analysis.one_liner: Taxes earnings above the Social Security payroll cap and raises retiree cost-of-living adjustments.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would gradually apply the Social Security payroll tax to all wages and give retirees a larger cost-of-living adjustment, was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change Social Security in two main ways. First, it would create a new Consumer Price Index for people 62 and older and use it to compute annual cost-of-living increases, since seniors' spending patterns (heavy on medical costs) typically produce higher measured inflation. Second, it would phase out the cap on wages subject to the Social Security payroll tax between 2014 and 2019, so that by 2020 every dollar of wages and self-employment income is taxed, with people who earn above the cap earning somewhat larger benefits for the extra contributions. It would also keep providing cash payments to beneficiaries in years when inflation produces no automatic increase.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and other Social Security beneficiaries age 62 and up, who would receive larger annual cost-of-living increases under the new elderly price index; the program itself, which would collect substantially more payroll tax revenue and be more solvent; and high-earning beneficiaries, who would earn modest additional benefits for their above-cap contributions. Beneficiaries would also receive cash payments in years without a COLA.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers tracking the spending of people 62 and older, and makes that index the basis for cost-of-living increases in benefits for people 62 and up.

Phases in taxation of wages and self-employment income above the contribution and benefit base: the share of above-cap earnings left untaxed falls from 86% in 2014 to 0% after 2019, so from 2020 all earnings are subject to the payroll tax.
Credits people who pay tax on above-cap earnings with additional benefits, at 3% and 0.25% factors on their surplus average indexed monthly earnings.
Continues cash payments to beneficiaries in years when no cost-of-living adjustment takes effect, extending the arrangement created by the 2009 recovery act's section 9001.

analysis.who_pays: The highest-earning workers and the self-employed, who would pay Social Security tax on wages above the annual cap in increasing amounts from 2014 through 2019 and on all wages from 2020, and their employers, who pay a matching share. High earners would receive small additional benefits, but far less than the added tax they would pay.

drawbacks.text: High earners would pay substantially more in payroll tax while receiving only small additional benefits (a 3% and 0.25% benefit factor on above-cap earnings), which critics of cap removal argue weakens the link between what individuals contribute and what they receive.
Employers would owe a matching 6.2% tax on wages above the cap once the phase-in is complete, raising labor costs at high-wage firms, which could be passed through to prices or wages.
The new elderly price index would require the Bureau of Labor Statistics to build and maintain a separate monthly index, with sums appropriated as necessary.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary beneficiaries the bill is strongly favorable: larger, more accurate cost-of-living increases for seniors, cash payments in no-COLA years, and a trust fund with more revenue behind it. The cost is concentrated and real — a large new tax burden on households and employers above the wage cap, only partly offset by extra benefits for the high earners themselves. The tradeoff is a straightforward choice about who finances the program, not a badly designed one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on February 13, 2013, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Begich introduced the Protecting and Preserving Social Security Act in the Senate on February 13, 2013.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record.
Two Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The Finance Committee held no hearing or markup and the Senate never voted on the bill before the 113th Congress ended January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and employers above the payroll-tax cap are better off, because the tax stayed limited to wages under the annual cap and retiree cost-of-living increases stayed tied to the general price index. Beneficiaries gained nothing from the bill's failure, but also lost nothing already in law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the tax cap

for.name: Sen. Mark Begich
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill in the Senate on February 13, 2013.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Max Baucus, D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it; it died in committee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three senators attached to the bill — Begich and his two cosponsors — were Democrats, no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever taken, so the split never surfaced on the floor.

industries.industry: High-earning households (wages and self-employment income above the annual Social Security tax cap)
industries.note: The bill phases in the payroll tax on all earnings above the cap, reaching full taxation by 2020; high earners would get small extra benefits but pay far more in tax. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against retirees' interest in bigger, better-funded benefits.

Employers pay a matching share of the Social Security tax, so extending the tax to wages above the cap would raise their payroll costs. Their savings from the bill's failure came out of the program's revenue side.

Not an industry, but the directly affected group: beneficiaries 62 and up would have received larger COLAs under the new elderly price index, plus cash payments in no-COLA years, and the trust fund would have gained revenue.
